# Issue #2194: A number read from a lock is taken by a spawned task as if it moved (NK2101 on a `Seen[i64]`), and the help's `.clone()` then draws a warning that it makes nothing new (NK1350)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2194).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-19 · 0 comments

Found while drafting "The lock tests of std move into Nikaia programs" (#2189). No item of it is blocked: its race program (item 5) races two `set(…; after:)` calls on a literal witness. A program that used `n.get()` as the witness in two tasks, the natural way to write the race, meets this defect.

## What happens today

Binary: `target/release/nikaia` (nikaia 0.1.0, built 2026-11-18 06:16 from `develop`), run in a scratch directory outside the checkout with `nikaia run FILE`. The same message at `--user-parallelism no` (exit 1) and `yes` (exit 101; a refused program elsewhere, such as a missing method, exits 1 at `yes`, so that exit code is a second thing to look at in item 1).

```nika
fn main() throws {
    let n: SharedMut[i64] = SharedMut(0)
    let seen = n.get()
    let a = spawn fn { n.set(1; after: seen) catch { return } }
    let b = spawn fn { n.set(2; after: seen) catch { return } }
    a.join()
    b.join()
    println(f"{n.get()}")
}
```

```
error[NK2101]: You're using `seen` after a background task took it.
  --> seen.nika:5:24
   |
 5 |     let b = spawn fn { n.set(2; after: seen) catch { return } }
   |                        ^
   |
   = note: A task started with `spawn` may outlive this function, so it takes the variables it uses with it. `seen` is a `Seen[i64]`, so it went to the task.
   = note: Numbers, `bool`s, views and `Shared[T]` handles aren't taken: they're copied.
   = help: Make a copy before and hand over the copy: `let copy = seen.clone()`, then use `copy` inside.
1 value a task took with it
```

Exit 1 at the default setting. The message contradicts itself: its second note says numbers are copied, and `seen` is a number. Following the help:

```nika
fn main() throws {
    let n: SharedMut[i64] = SharedMut(0)
    let seen = n.get()
    let seen2 = seen.clone()
    println(f"{seen2}")
}
```

```
warning[NK1350]: `seen` is an `i64`, which copies by itself: `.clone()` makes nothing new.
  --> seen_clone.nika:4:17
   |
 4 |     let seen2 = seen.clone()
   |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: A number, a `bool`, a `char` and a type whose every part copies are copied wherever they are read (ADR-294 D9.1).
   = help: Delete `.clone()`.
0
```

Variants, each run the same way:

* `let seen: i64 = n.get()` in the first program: accepted, prints `1`, exit 0.
* Two spawns that each run `println(f"{seen}")`, with no `set` at all: the same NK2101. So it is about the task, not the lock door.
* `async(detached)` in place of `spawn`: the same NK2101 ("after a detached task took it").
* Handing `seen` twice to `fn take(x: i64)` and putting it in two tuples, with no task: accepted, prints `1 1 0 0`.
* A `SharedMut[Vec[i64]]` read with `get` and used in two spawns: NK2101, rightly, since a `Vec` moves.

No open issue names it (searched the titles for `Seen` and task).

## Expected

* ADR-281 D22: `get` hands out `Seen[T]`, and the emitter erases the stamp: a `Seen[i64]` is an `i64` in the language below. D23: the stamp passes through what cannot write it back.
* ADR-294 D9.1, as NK1350 cites it: a number is copied wherever it is read. So a `Seen[i64]` is copied into each task, and the first program prints `1` or `2` (whichever `set` comes first; the other is overtaken).
* Part III C.1 and C.4: NK2101 stands in for rustc's "use of moved value". It is not asked of a value that copies.

## Cause

Traced in the code, not yet in a run; item 1 confirms it with a probe.

* `a_task_takes_these` (around line 175) and `takes_of_a_lambda` (around line 145) in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_lambdas.nika` record a local as taken when `takes_away(world, local.ty)` holds.
* `takes_away` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_values.nika` (line 12) starts with `moves_away(ty)`.
* `moves_away` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_types.nika` (line 142): for a `Ty::Named` it is true unless the name is a number, `bool`, `char`, `scalar`, `Shared` or `SharedMut`. `Seen` is none of these, so `Seen[i64]` moves away. `copies_plainly` (line 162) has the same gap. Neither looks through the stamp with `Ty::unseen()` (`crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/ty.nika`), as `Ty::fits` does.
* The note of NK2101 is built in `a_task_took_what_is_used_again` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_takes.nika` (around line 885) from `ty.shown()`, which is why it says `Seen[i64]`.

## To build

1. Confirm the cause: `nikaia run scripts/where.nika -- moves_away` and a probe that shows `moves_away` true for `Seen[i64]` and false for `i64`. A cause shown false is answered `wrong I7: ...` in the report.
2. Make `moves_away` and `copies_plainly` judge a stamped type by what it holds (`ty.unseen()`), so a `Seen[T]` moves exactly when `T` does. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_number_read_from_a_lock_is_copied_into_two_tasks.nika` with its `.stdout`: the first program above with `spawn`, a second pair with `async(detached)`, and a `bool` read with `get`; each prints its result, at both settings.
3. Keep the move of a stamped value that does move. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_list_read_from_a_lock_is_taken_by_the_first_task.nika` with its `.stderr`: a `Seen[Vec[i64]]` used in two spawns gives NK2101, its note naming the type.
4. Sweep for the rule (I10): the other callers of `moves_away` and `copies_plainly` (in `check_core_call_on.nika`, `check_core_flow.nika`, `check_core_leaves.nika`, `check_types.nika`, `check_values.nika` and `emit_exprs.nika`, 14 call sites) and any other test of a type's name that misses `Seen`. Name each one checked in the report; one that changes behaviour gets its case in the test of item 2.

## Done when

* The first program prints `1` or `2` and exits 0 at both settings, and `nikaia run` gives no NK2101 for the variants with a number or a `bool`.
* The tests of items 2 and 3 are green at both settings; the test of item 2 failed on the unfixed tree.
* The commit of item 4 carries `Fixes #N` (#N being this issue's number); the others say `Part of #N`.
* The report gives a `Found:` line for each defect met on the way.

## Files and limits

* `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_types.nika`, and what item 4 names; their lowered `.rs` is output.
* `tests/compiler/tests/` (the two programs and their `.stdout` / `.stderr`).
* No new Rust, no new Rust test, no new NK code.

## Ruled out

* The lock door: two spawns that only print `seen` fail the same way.
* The emitter: the checker refuses the program before anything is emitted.
* The message alone: the refusal itself is wrong, so changing the help without the check would still refuse a valid program.

# Issue #2195: A method called on a tuple or on `()` is refused as a type the compiler can't tell (NK1245), not as a method the type lacks (NK1171)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2195).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-19 · 0 comments

Found while drafting "The lock tests of std move into Nikaia programs" (#2189). No item of it waits for this: its programs use `set(…; after:)` under `catch`, as Part I 7.1 asks, and never call a method on the result. A reader who expects `set` to hand back a `Result` (and calls `.is_ok()` on it) meets this message instead of one that says what is wrong.

## What happens today

Binary: `target/release/nikaia` (nikaia 0.1.0, built 2026-11-18 06:16 from `develop`), run in a scratch directory outside the checkout with `nikaia run FILE`.

```nika
fn main() throws {
    let n: SharedMut[Vec[i64]] = SharedMut([0])
    let r = n.set([1]; after: [0])
    println(f"{r.is_ok()}")
}
```

```
error[NK1245]: The compiler can't tell what type `r.is_ok()` is.
  --> isok.nika:4:5
   |
 4 |     println(f"{r.is_ok()}")
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: What is not known is not checked, so a type nothing can tell is refused rather than left to the language below.
   = help: Write the type down where the value is made, such as `let x: T = …`, or pass it to a parameter that declares one.
1 type error
```

Exit 1. The compiler does know the type of `r`: `set` hands back nothing, so `r` is `()`. The help asks for a type annotation, which cannot help.

The same NK1245, with nothing of the lock in it:

* `let r = n.set([1])` (a plain `set`): NK1245 on `r.is_ok()`.
* `fn noop() { let _x = 1 }`, then `let r = noop()` and `r.is_ok()`: NK1245.
* `let t = (1, 2)`, then `t.is_ok()`: NK1245 on `t.is_ok()`.

The same call on other types gives the right refusal:

* `let r: i64 = 3`, then `r.is_ok()`: `error[NK1210]: \`i64\` has no method called \`is_ok\`.`
* `struct P { x: i64 }`, then `p.is_ok()`: `error[NK1171]: \`P\` has no method called \`is_ok\`.`

No open issue names it (searched the titles for NK1245 with tuple and with method).

## Expected

* Part III, the table of codes in `docs/specification/30-nikaia-tooling.md`: NK1171 is a member nothing writes down; NK1245 is an expression whose type the compiler cannot tell (C.4). The type of `r` and of `t` is known, so the refusal is NK1171.
* For the probes: `error[NK1171]: \`()\` has no method called \`is_ok\`.` and `error[NK1171]: \`(i64, i64)\` has no method called \`is_ok\`.`, each with the note `a_member_is_refused` gives a type with no members.
* Part I 7.1: a door of a lock fails by a throw caught with `catch`; there is no `Result` to ask. A note that says so where the type is `()` and the method is `is_ok` / `is_err` is welcome but not required.

## Cause

Suspected, from reading the code; item 1 checks it with a probe.

* `check_core_call_on` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_core_call_on.nika` ends a call it does not know with `state.a_member_nothing_writes_down(world, type_name, entry, true, span)` (around line 412).
* `type_name` comes from `check_core_call_on_type_name` (line 125), which names a `Ty::Named`, a `Seq` and a slice, and gives `""` for anything else, a `Ty::Tuple` among them (`()` is `Ty::Tuple([])`).
* `a_member_nothing_writes_down` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_members.nika` (line 148) returns at once when the head is not declared (`if !declared { return }`); `""` is never declared. Nothing is refused, the call's type stays `Ty::Unknown`, and the later C.4 check refuses it as NK1245.

## To build

1. Check the cause: `nikaia run scripts/where.nika -- check_core_call_on_type_name` and a probe that prints the head `a_member_nothing_writes_down` receives for `t.is_ok()` (expected `""`). A cause shown false is answered `wrong I7: ...` in the report.
2. Refuse a method on a tuple or on `()` that no std entry and no trait provides as NK1171, naming the type as `Ty::shown()` writes it. The tuple methods std does describe (if any; item 1 lists them) stay accepted. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_method_on_a_tuple_or_nothing_is_refused_as_missing.nika` with its `.stderr`: `is_ok` on the result of `set(…; after:)`, on the result of a function without a result, and on `(1, 2)`; each gives NK1171, none NK1245.
3. Sweep for the rule (I10): the other refusals in `check_core_call_on` that take `type_name` (`nothing_says_what_a_parameter_can_do`, `no_number_has_this_method`, `a_list_collected`) and the path and field checks in `check_members.nika` (`t.name` on a tuple, `().x`): each that ends in NK1245 for a known type is fixed alike, with its case in the test of item 2. Name each one checked in the report.

## Done when

* The three probes give NK1171 naming `()` or `(i64, i64)`, exit 1, and no NK1245.
* `int_m` still gives NK1210 and `struct_m` still NK1171.
* The test of item 2 is green; it failed on the unfixed tree.
* The commit of item 3 carries `Fixes #N` (#N being this issue's number); the others say `Part of #N`.
* The report gives a `Found:` line for each defect met on the way.

## Files and limits

* `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_core_call_on.nika` and `check_members.nika`; their lowered `.rs` is output.
* `tests/compiler/tests/` (the program and its `.stderr`).
* No new Rust, no new Rust test, no new NK code: NK1171 exists.

## Ruled out

* The lock: a function without a result and a plain tuple give the same NK1245.
* A wrong type for `r`: `let r = n.get()` with `r.is_ok()` on a `SharedMut[i64]` gives NK1210 for `i64`, so the type flows; only the tuple head is lost.

# Issue #2198: Pipes, redirections and `&&` as a structure, not a shell text: a list of commands with their arguments and where each stream goes

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2198).

`note`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-19 · 0 comments

Follows from "Decision: which shell `process::shell` runs on Windows" (#1937), owner, 2026-11-19, [ADR-raw-sinks-1](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-raw-sinks-1.md) D9 item 3.

## Goal

What a program wants a shell for (a pipe `a | b`, a redirection `> file`, `&&` / `||`, a glob) is given later as a structure: a list of commands, each a program with its arguments, and where each stream goes. A value from outside is always one argument, so nothing is escaped and nothing has to be proved. It runs without a shell, the same on every platform. A sketch of the shape, not decided:

```nika
use std::process

let out = process::pipe([process::cmd("convert", [name, "-resize", "64x64", "-"]),
                         process::cmd("gzip", [])];
                        stdout: process::to_file("thumb.png.gz"))
```

A library that does hand a text to `sh` or `cmd.exe` is the shell library ADR-raw-sinks-1 keeps the `untrusted-shell` key for (D4, D5): its escaping is its own, and the application allows it.

## Open before it can be `ready`

* `std` or an official package (ADR-289 D2: is a pipeline an operating-system resource or a library on top of `process::run`?).
* The form of the structure, of `&&` / `||` and of a glob, written as an ADR.
* An argument that starts with `-` is not solved by this: "Decision: an outside argument that starts with `-` is read as an option" (#1939).

Status `note` until a program needs it; then it becomes a `decision` with a decision paper.

# Issue #2241: A block without `-> T` gets a row type the compiler writes from the row its grammar describes

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2241).

`libraries`, `blocked`, `database` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-22 · 0 comments

## Goal

A `dsl` block without `-> T` gets a row type the compiler writes from the `row` its grammar describes (ADR-323 D3, D5; ADR-299 D2, D22). `q.execute(db)` then hands back rows with fields: `u.name`, `u.a.id`. This comes after the declared-struct form "`dsl … -> T { … } eod`" (#477), by the owner's order of 2026-11-19: a program can read rows into its own struct first, and the type written from data comes last.

Part of #89
Needs #114
After #477

## Governing decisions

- [ADR-323](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-323.md) D5: the grammar's entry returns `meta::Statement { row, parameters }`; a namespace is a field whose type is a `Record`. D3: `Text` is `String`, `Maybe(T)` is `T?`, `List(T)` is `Vec[T]`, `Record` a struct. D4: a message names the block and the grammar; `--comptime` prints the type.
- [ADR-299](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-299.md) D22 (owner, 2026-11-19; it restates D12 and D13 without tables): the row is the record the grammar describes. A namespace's fields are reached through it (`u.a.id`). A field one level down is also reached by its own name (`u.name`) where nothing else in the row answers to that name; otherwise the short name is `NK1107`, and the help names the full paths. Deeper fields only by their full path. D14: the grammar refuses a name that cannot be a field.
- Not decided ([ADR-323](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-323.md) §6): whether two blocks with the same columns share one type. Until it is: each block its own type.

## Today

After #114, a statement block's `execute` hands back `Vec[db::Row]`, and `--comptime` shows the row and parameter types the grammar described. No row type is written. The conversion of a `db::Row` into a typed row and `db::NullInField` (`packages/db/src/main.nika`) are not used by the compiler.

## To build

1. **The row struct.** For a statement block without `-> T`, write a struct from the described `row`: one nested struct per namespace (a field whose type is a `Record`), and the short names one level down by D22's rule. `execute` returns `Vec[<that struct>]`. Each block gets its own type.
   Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_blocks_rows_have_its_columns_as_fields.nika` with `.stdout`. A stub grammar describes namespaces `a { id: I64, name: Text, email: Maybe(Text) }` and `b { id: I64 }`. A fake connection returns rows, and the program reads `u.name`, `u.email ?? "-"`, `u.a.id`, `u.b.id`.
2. **The conversion** (ADR-299 D8, D18). Each `db::Row` becomes the struct. A `Null` in a field that is not `T?` fails `execute` with `db::NullInField`, naming the field and the column.
   Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_null_in_a_field_that_is_no_option_fails_execute.nika` with `.stdout`.
3. **The messages** (D22, ADR-323 D4). `u.id` where `a` and `b` both have `id` is `NK1107`, with help naming `u.a.id` and `u.b.id`. `u.emial` is `NK1107`, naming the block's line and the fields. A field two levels down read by its short name is `NK1107`, naming its full path.
   Test: `tests/compiler/tests/a_shared_or_misspelled_column_names_the_ways.nika` with `.stderr`.
4. **`--comptime` prints the written row type** of each block, beside #114's description.

## Done when

`for u in q.execute(db) { println(u.name) }` builds and runs on a statement block without `-> T`. `u.id` over two namespaces with `id` is `NK1107`, and the help names both paths. The commit of item 3 carries `Fixes #N`. The report gives one `Found:` line per finding.

## Files

The emitter's statement path that #114 adds, `check_fields.nika` (field access on the written type), `project_check.nika` (item 4), and their lowered files. Not touched: `packages/db`, #477's `-> T` path.

# Issue #2245: A grammar naming a rule it does not have is refused as a compiler bug (`NK1178`), not as the program's mistake

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2245).

`ready`, `bugs` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-22 · 0 comments

## What happens

A grammar that names a rule which neither the grammar declares nor Part II 10.8 offers as a built-in is not refused by the checker. The name reaches the generated parser, and the backend refuses it there.

- Where the grammar runs while the program is built (`dsl G { … } eod`, a `comptime`), the user gets `NK1178` with *This is a bug in the compiler, not in your program* and the backend's `Undefined rule`.
- Where it runs with the program, the user gets the backend's `error: Undefined rule: 'nmae'.`, without a code.

A rule called with values is refused properly (`NK1171`). The same misspelling without values is not.

Found while "A grammar declares a statement's columns and parameters" (#114) was being rewritten (a probe with `alpha`, which is no built-in; `alpha1` is).

## Probe

Run on `target/fast/nikaia` of `6c4b12ab`, in the shared checkout, with `nikaia check p.nika`:

```nika
grammar G {
    entry rule r -> String = s:nmae -> { s }
}

fn main() throws {
    let x = dsl G { abc } eod
    println(x)
}
```

**Expected** (the checker, before any parser is generated, in the words `NK1171` already uses for a rule called with values):

```
error[NK1171]: Grammar `G` has no rule called `nmae`.
```

**Actual:**

```
error[NK1178]: The parser generated for `G::r` didn't compile.
   = note: This is a bug in the compiler, not in your program.
    error: Undefined rule: 'nmae'
```

Shapes run:
- `s:nmae`, `s:alpha` and `s:text(alpha+)` in a `dsl` block: all `NK1178` as above.
- `G::r("abc")` called at run time (no build-time run): `error: Undefined rule: 'nmae'.` from the backend, at the right line, no `NK` code.
- Working: `s:raw_ident` in its place builds and prints `abc`.
- Working: a rule called with values and misspelled, `v:piar(1)` beside `rule pair(a: i64)`, is `error[NK1171]: Grammar `G` has no rule called `piar`.`

## Governing decision

Part III's code table: `NK1171` is *a member a known head or receiver does not have*, and the checker already uses it for a grammar's rule called with values (`grammar_call` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_grammar.nika`). Part II 10.8 (*The Grammar's Vocabulary*) lists the built-ins. `NK1178` says the generated parser not compiling is *this compiler's defect*, which is the mismatch: the defect is in the program, and the compiler should say so in its own words.

## Cause

`suspected`: `reference_type` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_grammar.nika` returns `Ty::Unknown` for a `Pattern::Ref` that is no rule of the grammar and none of the built-ins it knows, and refuses nothing. Only `grammar_call` (a reference with values) refuses an unknown name. Check that settles it: a refusal in `reference_type`'s fall-through turns the probe into `NK1171`.

The list of built-ins `reference_type` knows is not the whole of Part II 10.8 (it types some, and lets others through as `Unknown`). So the refusal needs the full list of 10.8's names, not just the ones `reference_type` types.

## To build

1. A `Pattern::Ref` without values that names no rule of the grammar and no built-in of Part II 10.8 is `NK1171`: *Grammar `G` has no rule called `nmae`.* The help names the nearest rule or built-in where one is close (as `nearest_parameter` in `dsl.nika` does for parameters), else *Declare the rule, or use a built-in of Part II 10.8.* The list of built-ins is one list in `check_grammar.nika`, used by this check and by `reference_type`.
   Test: `tests/compiler/tests/grammar_an_unknown_rule_is_refused.nika` with `.stderr`, covering `s:nmae` (help: `name` declared beside it) and `s:text(alpha+)` (help: `alpha1`).
2. The grammars in the tree still build: `nikaia test` on `tests/compiler/tests/grammar_*.nika` and the packages with grammars (`json`, `yaml`, `logic`) shows no new refusal. A built-in the list misses is added to the list, not worked around.

## Done when

The probe is refused with `NK1171` naming `nmae`, by the checker, and no grammar in the tree is refused. The commit of item 1 carries `Fixes #N`. The report gives one `Found:` line per finding.

## Files

`crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/check_grammar.nika` and its lowered file. Not touched: the emitter (`emit_grammar.nika`) and `NK1178`'s other cases.

`decision`, `adr` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-20 · 0 comments

## Goal

After the grammar, database, views and collections records, about 190 numbered records and a few topic records with a count (`regex-1`, `async-5`, …) remain. Each needs its topic before it can be consolidated (ADR-decision-records-v2 D2, D4), and the owner confirms the topics (#904).

ADR-decision-records-v2 D1, D2, D4.

## Today

`ls docs/specification/adr/adr-[0-9]*.md | wc -l` gives 196 at commit 443a4f4b; the grammar and database issues take seven of them (177, 296, 299, 323, 339, 366, 388).

## To build

1. **The table**, in this issue's body (the issue is the record): every live record, the topic it joins (one to three words, the general one first, as `grammar-syntax`), grouped by the index sections. A record that covers several topics is split by decision, as ADR-296 was. A topic record with a count keeps its name until it is changed (`regex-1`, then `regex-v2`, D4) and is listed only where it shares a topic with a numbered record.

Every live record that is not a `-v` record has a confirmed topic in this issue's table, and each topic has its consolidation issue; this issue is closed by hand when the last one is filed.

No file changes; the result is the table and the issues.

Consolidating whatever a change happens to touch, without a table: topics would be cut differently each time.

# Issue #2276: Open issues cite the consolidated ADRs by their new names

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2276).

`blocked`, `adr` · opened 2026-11-19 · updated 2026-11-19 · 0 comments

Part of #904
Needs #2274

## Goal

Open issues are work orders; a builder follows `ADR-323 D5` into a record that is no longer live. After the grammar, database, views and collections consolidations, the open issues are rewritten by the same tables. Closed issues and commit messages stay as written: the history row finds what they meant (ADR-decision-records-v2 D3).

## Governing decision

ADR-decision-records-v2 D3; #904 step 6.

## Today

Known open issues citing a source:
- "A statement's grammar returns its description, and the block runs on a connection" (#114)
- "`dsl … -> T { … } eod`" (#477)
- "A block without `-> T` gets a row type the compiler writes from the row its grammar describes" (#2241)
- "A grammar naming a rule it does not have is refused as a compiler bug" (#2245)

The full list comes from the search in item 1.

## To build

1. **The list**: every open issue whose body cites a source record of #2264 to #2274 (`gh api -X GET search/issues -f q='repo:Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia is:issue is:open "ADR-296"'`, one search per source).
2. **Dry run**: each body through the tool of #2262 (`--dry-run` on a file holding the body); the changes are listed in a comment here before anything is written.
3. **Write**: the bodies updated through the GitHub API (supervisor; builders do not write to GitHub). Comments are not edited; a comment that matters gets a reply naming the new decision.

This issue is repeated in the same form for each batch #2275 files.

## Done when

No open issue body cites a source record of #2264 to #2274, checked by the searches of item 1; closed by hand.

## Files and limits

No repository file changes. Closed issues, comments and commit messages are not rewritten.

## What was ruled out

Rewriting closed issues and commit messages: history is read as it was written, and the history README maps it.

## What

The compiler (`crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/*.nika`), `scripts/*.nika` and `examples/` / `packages/` pass the raw path sink check (NK1308, brought to develop behind warn by #2303) by proof, not by `trusted:` (ADR-raw-sinks-1 D13, D14, D15, D16; owner's decision on #2242, 2026-11-19): each site is looked at alone. A name from `fs::read_dir` is opened under `root.join(dir)`; a name from outside that must be one component is guarded with `path::is_component`; a relative path that must stay below a root with `path::is_below`; a temporary directory comes from `fs::scratch()`. What is the tool's job (`nikaia build FILE` opens the file it is given) is said once in the manifest by a D15 line with a comment, e.g. `untrusted-paths-read = ["args"]`, never `trusted:` at a site.

Part of #2242
Needs #2300
Needs #2303

for name in fs::read_dir(dir, fs::Root::Anywhere) {

becomes

let tests = root.join(dir)
for name in fs::read_dir(".", tests) {

ADR-raw-sinks-1 D13, D14, D15, D16.2 (nikaia's own D15 line with a comment), D16.3 (what no form covers is reported, not written around).

# Issue #2379: A program counts its allocations only where it reads the counts or sets a budget

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2379).

`runtime`, `performance`, `decision` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-20 · 0 comments

Found while a Counting global allocator in the nikaia binary costs +4.2 % instructions (#2368)
Part of std::mem: allocations() and usage() per thread (ADR-400) (#2112)

## Goal
A program pays for counting its allocations only where it reads the counts. Today every emitted program and (with #2368) the `nikaia` binary installs `task_block::Counting` (`crates/unsafe/task-block/src/lib.rs`), which on every `alloc`, `dealloc` and `realloc` adds to the thread's `TALLY` (ADR-400 D1, D2) and to the running block's `outside` (ADR-327 D9, D10).

## Measured (callgrind, a compile of `tests/compiler/tests/byteset_every_search_is_the_byte_by_byte_one.nika`)
* system allocator: 4,439,441,817 Ir; Counting: 4,608,631,081 Ir (+3.81 %).
* about 6.05 M alloc, 6.04 M dealloc and 0.88 M realloc calls: about 13 Ir per call. `__rust_alloc` grows from a jump to `malloc` to a framed function with two thread-local updates (the TLS reads are already direct `%fs` offsets, no `__tls_get_addr`).

## To decide
* Who needs the counts: a program that calls `std::mem::allocations()` / `usage()`, a test block that does, and a task with a memory budget (ADR-327 D15 reads `outside`).
* Options: (a) the compiler installs `Counting` only where the program (its closure of called functions) reaches `mem::allocations`, `mem::usage` or a budget, the system allocator otherwise; (b) one allocator with a counting switch read per call (cheaper, not free); (c) keep counting always and make it cheaper (one thread-local, count before the call so `malloc` is a tail call).
* Recommendation: (a), with (c)'s cheaper path for programs that count.

## Done when
A program that reads no counts and sets no budget runs with the system allocator (instruction count equal to it, measured), and one that reads them still gets ADR-400's numbers (`tests/compiler/tests/` test).

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2382).

`compiler`, `performance`, `blocked` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-20 · 4 comments

Found while a Counting global allocator in the nikaia binary costs +4.2 % instructions (#2368)

## Goal
The compiler allocates less. In a compile of `tests/compiler/tests/byteset_every_search_is_the_byte_by_byte_one.nika` (callgrind, nikaia built from develop with the system allocator, 4,439,441,817 Ir in all) glibc's allocator alone takes about 31 %:

| function | Ir |
|---|---|
| `_int_free` | 413,726,467 |
| `_int_malloc` | 350,735,000 |
| `malloc` | 280,007,027 |
| `free` | 169,201,028 |
| `malloc_consolidate` | 67,425,282 |
| `realloc` | 54,453,074 |

for about 6.05 M allocations, 6.04 M frees and 0.88 M reallocations. Visible callers in the same profile: `core::fmt::write` with `Text as Write` (text built by formatting), `List<u8, Place>::grow`, `BTreeMap<Text, _>::insert` and its `IntoIter::dying_next`, `StrSearcher::new`, `proofs_write_term`, `text_tiers`.

## To build
1. Count allocations per compiler phase and per call site (the inclusive cost of `malloc` per caller in callgrind) and list the ten largest sites here.
2. For each: the change in the `.nika` source (`crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/*.nika`) that removes the allocation (reuse a buffer, build text once, a view instead of a copy), or the compiler defect that makes the lowering allocate where the source does not (fixed in the compiler, ADR-294).
3. Measure before and after each step (`docs/measuring.md`).

## Done when
The ten largest sites are handled or filed, and the compile above spends at most half the Ir in the allocator it spends today.

# Issue #2383: Rethink how programs get, reuse and free memory (arenas, pools, reuse, deferred frees), measured

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2383).

`runtime`, `performance`, `decision` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-20 · 0 comments

Found while a Counting global allocator in the nikaia binary costs +4.2 % instructions (#2368)
Related: Choosing the allocator: a build, a task or a call names where memory comes from, and an allocation that may fail returns a value (#1493); ADR-327 D4-D11: memory budgets per task and per shared value (#490)

## Goal
Rethink how Nikaia programs get, reuse and give back memory, beyond allocating less (the issue on the compiler allocating less). About 31 % of a compile's instructions are glibc's `malloc`/`free`; a task's block (ADR-327) already bump-allocates inside a segment, and everything outside it goes to the system allocator.

## To find out (a study, measured)
* Where values live: which allocations could go into the task's block, an arena per phase, or a pool per size, freed all at once at its end instead of one by one.
* Reuse: buffers and lists cleared and kept instead of dropped and allocated again; what the language could say about it (ownership already knows the last use).
* Freeing: frees deferred to the end of a block or phase; `malloc_consolidate` (67 M Ir in the compile above) points at fragmentation.
* Other allocators (a size-class allocator in place of glibc), measured against the same compile.

## Done when
A decision paper (options with measured figures, a recommendation) is attached here and the chosen steps are filed as issues.

# Issue #2417: yaml: events and nodes refer to their scalars in the input instead of copying each into a String

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2417).

`blocked`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-23 · 18 comments

Filed by the supervisor (owner's goal, 2026-11-20: yaml faster than saphyr-parser).

Part of #1548.

## Goal

An event and a tree node hold their text as a view of the input instead of an owned `String`. Then a scalar costs no allocation and no copy between the parse and the walk.

## Today

- `pub struct Event` in packages/yaml/src/main.nika holds `value: String`, `text: String?`, `anchor: String?` and `tag: String?`. `walk` fills them from the `Node` tree, which holds its own `String` per scalar.
- So each scalar is allocated at least twice: once in the node, once in its event.
- `benches/yaml/README.md`, *Where yaml is behind*: `malloc` and `free` are about 11 % of `deep` with checks off (callgrind on `target/yaml-bench/bin/events.off`).

## To build

- [ ] Measure first: callgrind on `events.off` with `deep` and `large` at today's `develop`. Report the inclusive share of `malloc`/`free`/`memcpy` and how much of it comes from scalar strings.
- [ ] Check what ADR-views-v4 allows: can a `pub struct` returned from a package hold a view of the caller's input (`from`, a lent field)? Can the `@stream` entry's emitted items do the same?
  - Where the language allows neither, stop: `Result: blocked`, `Found:` with a probe of a few lines, `Needs: supervisor decision`.
- [ ] Build the views:
  - A plain or quoted scalar without escapes or folding refers to its bytes in the input.
  - Only a scalar whose value differs from its source text (escapes, folding, block chomping) owns a `String`.
- [ ] Re-run `nikaia run benches/yaml/bench.nika` and update the table in `benches/yaml/README.md`.

## Done when

- Events and nodes take no `String` for a scalar whose value is its source text.
- `events.off` counts fewer instructions on `deep`, `large` and `scalars` (figures from callgrind in the commit message).
- Outputs stay byte-identical. The package's tests and the yaml-test-suite pass list are green.

# Issue #2419: winnow-grammar picks an alternative by the first byte where the alternatives' first bytes are disjoint

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2419).

`wip`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-20 · 1 comment

Filed by the supervisor (owner's goal, 2026-11-20: yaml faster than saphyr-parser).

Part of #1548.

## Goal

winnow-grammar picks an alternative by the input's first byte where the alternatives' first bytes do not overlap, instead of trying them in turn. This helps every grammar written in Nikaia. Built in winnow-grammar (keywan-ghadami/winnow-grammar) and pinned in Nikaia, as for #2293.

## Today

- `benches/yaml/README.md`, *Where yaml is behind*: the choices of `FlowItem` and `FlowAny` and `winnow_grammar::rt::expected` are 15 % of `deep` (callgrind, `events.off`, checks off).
- winnow-grammar already has `rt::first_byte` for some alternatives: it appears in the profile of `MapEntry`.
- Which alternatives it does not cover, and why, is not known yet.

## To build

- [ ] Measure first: with callgrind on `events.off deep` and `large`, list the alternatives of the yaml grammar by inclusive cost. Note which of them `first_byte` covers in the generated code (winnow-grammar-macros, codegen of alternatives).
- [ ] In winnow-grammar, widen the first-byte dispatch:
  - to alternatives whose first sets are known after optional or trivia elements;
  - to sets of more than one byte (a 256-entry table);
  - with a fallback that tries in turn where the sets overlap.
  - Messages must stay byte-identical (ADR 17: the dispatch is a fast-pass decision; the diagnosing pass may keep trying in turn).
- [ ] winnow-grammar's tests green, `examples/stream_profile.rs` and a yaml profile measured; PR on winnow-grammar.
- [ ] Pin Nikaia to it (both `Cargo.toml` and both lock files); re-run `benches/yaml/bench.nika` and update the README table.

## Done when

- The alternatives of `FlowItem`, `FlowAny` and `Block` dispatch by first byte where their first sets are disjoint.
- `events.off deep` counts fewer instructions.
- All winnow-grammar and Nikaia tests are green, and the outputs are byte-identical.

_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2419#issuecomment-7042114440)

First measurement (supervisor session, winnow-grammar branch `first-bytes-fixpoint`, commits 1cf41ae and f15a5ed). Result: **no gain for yaml**.

**What the branch builds.** The first-byte sets in `first_bytes.rs` now reach almost every rule of the yaml grammar:
- Rules with value parameters get a set; before, a rule with any parameter got none.
- A pattern argument is put in place of its parameter (`__nikaia_count(p = " ")`).
- `count`, `empty`, `eof`, `any`, `text`, `bytes` and `span` are handled.
- `peek(p)` fixes the byte, so a cut after it no longer blocks the set (`SeqLevel`, `MapLevel`).
- The sets are a least fixed point, so a recursive rule (a node inside a node) gets a set instead of none.

winnow-grammar's tests stay 511/511, with new unit tests.

**Measured with callgrind** on `events.off` (opt 3, lto, checks off). Outputs are byte-identical:

| Input | Before | After |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| deep | 140.61M | 140.45M |
| scalars | 210.82M | 211.86M |
| large | 4,494.95M | 4,500.53M |

**Why it does not help.** The costly alternatives (`Block`, `Content`, `Inline`, `FlowItem`, `FlowAny`, `FlowNode`, `KeyNode`) reach a plain scalar early. A plain scalar begins with `x:any if(plain_safe(...))`, and its first set is every byte, so their sets are full and no guard is written. Where a set is narrow (`Seq`'s `-`, `KeyTail`), the guard costs about what it saves.

The two commits are reverted on the PR branch (keywan-ghadami/winnow-grammar#39, 15047c5) and kept on `first-bytes-fixpoint` for a grammar where they help.

**Where the 15 % of the alternatives does lie.** The alternatives repeat work they share:
- `Block`'s three alternatives each run `not(Marker) m:__nikaia_count(p = " ")` again before their guard.
- `Content` and `Spaced` each try `Seq`, `Map`, `Propped` and so on, which read the same properties and indentation.

Two directions follow:
- **(a) In the grammar.** Each rule reads the shared prefix once, as "packages/yaml counts each line's indentation twice" (#2411) does for `Blanks`/`Block`.
- **(b) In winnow-grammar.** The engine factors out a leading sequence that the alternatives of a rule share verbatim, with the same bindings, and parses it once.

I'll measure (b) next on the profile: how much of `Block`, `Content` and `Inline` is the repeated prefix. This issue stays `wip`.

## Done when

The program passes 200 runs in a row at user-parallelism = yes on 2 cores.

# Issue #2425: A mut parameter may receive views of another parameter, inferred (ADR-views-v4 D32)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2425).

`wip`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-20 · updated 2026-11-23 · 11 comments

Filed by the driver from the `Found:` of the run of `issue-2417` (#2417). Decided by the owner on 2026-11-21 and recorded as ADR-views-v4 D32 (38ad2cf3).

Part of #1548.

## Decision

A function may put a view of another lent parameter into a `mut` parameter: an element pushed, a field set, a value inserted. It may already hand one back as its result (D8).
- The source is **inferred** from the body, as for a result. Nothing is written at the parameter or at the call.
- `from` is written only where there is no body: a trait's method, a function type, a foreign or Rust function (D14's places). The form is `fn(n: Node, mut out: Vec[Event] from n)`.
- The caller treats the argument passed for `n` as D9 treats an argument a result views, for as long as what it passed for the `mut` parameter lives. It may give the argument up, but may not change it or hand it over.
- A `mut` parameter is no longer inferred `keep` because the body stores such a view.

## Probe

```nika
struct N {
	raw: String,
}
struct E {
	v: String,
}
fn walk(n: N, mut out: Vec[E]) {
	out.push(E { v: n.raw })
}
fn events(ns: Vec[N]) -> Vec[E] {
	let mut out: Vec[E] = []
	for n in ns {
		walk(n, out)
	}
	return out
}
fn make() -> String {
	let mut g = String()
	g.push_str("abc def")
	return g
}
fn main() throws {
	let ns = [N { raw: make() }]
	let es = events(ns)
	println(es[0].v)
}
```

Expected output: `abc def`, and `walk` lowers to `fn walk<'a>(n: &'a N, out: &mut Vec<E<'a>>)` with no clone of `raw`.

## Where it stands (2026-11-23, supervisor)

- Item 1 (a whole `String` parameter as the source) is built: a54a3365 / 4cd47895.
- The field forms the lent-struct issue blocked are built: aba7482c (a field of a lent struct parameter into a `mut` parameter or a handed-back struct) and a2b3adcf (a field of a `for` binding over a lent list). The builder of a2b3adcf reports that `walk(n: Node, mut out: Vec[Event]) { out.push(Event { value: n.raw }) }` lowers to `fn walk<'a>(n: &'a Node, out: &mut Vec<Event<'a>>)`.
- What is left of that issue (a view pushed into a *local* list) is not needed here.

The run checks the probe on today's `develop` first. If it prints `abc def` with the lowering above, the run adds the probe as a test and finishes the issue; otherwise it builds what is missing of item 2.

## To build

1. **Checker and caller, a whole `String` parameter as the source.** Built (a54a3365); the tests `a_view_of_a_lent_parameter_stored_into_a_mut_parameter_keeps_nothing` and `a_caller_may_not_change_what_a_mut_parameter_views` exist.
2. **A lent struct parameter as the source, and the lowering.** A field of a lent struct parameter (`n.raw`) stored into a `mut` parameter makes the struct parameter a source; the lowering gives the source parameter and the `mut` parameter's element type a shared lifetime.
   - Test: the probe, printing `abc def`, with `walk` lowering as above and no clone of `raw`.

## Done when

The probe prints `abc def` with no copy of the text in the lowering, the tests of both items are green, and the existing `--filter view` and `--filter keep` tests stay green. The commit of item 2 (or of the probe's test, where item 2 already holds) is the one that finishes this issue.

## Split (2026-11-21)

- `mut out: T from n` written where there is no body, and Part I's sentences on what a mut parameter receives (ADR-views-v4 D32): its own issue.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-20](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2425#issuecomment-7044139177)

#### Decision paper (supervisor, 2026-11-20)

**Origin.** This is part 2 of the owner's goal: yaml faster than saphyr-parser ("yaml: events and nodes refer to their scalars in the input instead of copying each into a String", #2417).

yaml's events would hold views of the input instead of copying each scalar. The walk fills one output list: `walk(n: Node, ds, mut out: Vec[Event])`. That shape fixed the copying once per level in #1548.

To put a view of `n` into `out`, the language has to say that the elements of `out` view `n`. ADR-views-v4 D8 and D14 give `from` to results only. A `mut` parameter that receives such an element gets `n` inferred as `keep` (NK1102), so the probe in this issue is refused.

On `large`, the strings of the events cost `walk` 4.87 % in malloc and `fold` 2.85 % in new `String`s (callgrind, `events.off`).

**Options**

1. **Do nothing.** Events keep owning their text. That is about 7–8 % of `large` left unused toward the goal.
2. **`from` on a `mut` parameter, written:** `fn walk(n: Node, ds: Vec[Dir], mut out: Vec[Event] from n)`.
   - It reads as "what this function puts into `out` views `n`".
   - The body is checked against it as D8 checks a result.
   - A caller treats the argument passed for `out` as a view of the argument passed for `n`, under the rules of D9: the source may be given up but not changed while `out` lives.
   - Rust: `fn walk<'a>(n: &'a Node, out: &mut Vec<Event<'a>>)`.
3. **The same, inferred** (D8's walk, kept per element of a `mut` parameter), with the written `from` optional, as on results. The signature no longer shows it, so a change to the body changes what callers may do.
4. **Return instead of filling**: each level returns its `Vec[Event]`. Results already carry `from`, but that is the per-level copy #1548 removed (deep went from 5.4× to 2.5× saphyr).

**Other languages.** Rust says this with a lifetime on the `&mut` collection (`&mut Vec<T<'a>>`). Swift and Kotlin have no views. C++ `std::string_view` into an output vector is unchecked.

**Recommendation: 2.** D8's `from` already states the source of a view on a result. Extending it to what a `mut` parameter receives is the same statement in the one other place a function can hand a view out. Written rather than inferred, because a caller's freedom with its arguments should be visible in the signature. Option 3 can follow as a convenience, with the written form as the rule.

Nikaia does not copy behind the programmer's back, and the region analysis already knows when memory is freed, as the fix for #2348 showed. So before the run-or-kept rule is written, each case gets its cheapest shape, with a probe and a callgrind figure:

3. **Kept, but the keeper dies inside the caller's region.** In the probe, `b` lives and dies inside `twice`. It can be lent with a lifetime, the way a returned box was built in the caller's block in the fix for #2348.
4. **Exactly one concrete lambda reaches the type in the package.** Monomorphise it: no `dyn` and no heap.
5. **Kept and it escapes upward, or is given to a task.** It is moved to the heap once, as a `Box`, not an `Arc`. An `Arc` is used only where ownership is really shared (ADR-312 D1).
6. **A `pub` boundary with unknown foreign lambdas.** The narrowest contract that still covers cases 1–5, following D17 (NK1264, NK1265).

No new keyword (ADR-277 D8: nothing is written). The rule is inferred, and the ledger shows which shape each position got and why. The next step is a study that measures each case on the probe and in the compiler's own call sites; it then gives the ADR text and the build items for #1121.

# Issue #2474: The corpus-wide ledger tests are 4-6x slower in CI since the panics inference goes through loops

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2474).

`blocked`, `ci` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-28 · 19 comments

Part of the ci lane's goal, a short CI run. Found while measuring the shards after "CI builds std only once" (#2082). Takes over the Founds of "the ledger's loop proof spends its cost in bounds_returns" (#2487) and "one function's walk blows up" (#2488), closed as duplicates of this one.

Facts: Ledger and bounds proofs, CI and caches

## What happens today

Since 0.0.1511 the tests that check the whole corpus through the ledger take 4-6 times as long in CI. Per-test times from the CI logs, before → after:

* heavy-rest: `bytes::the_corpus_needs_no_tether` (`crates/nikaia/tests/it/bytes.rs:268`) 108 s → 676 s.
* heavy-rest: `contracts::a_toolchain_module_is_not_part_of_std` (`crates/nikaia/tests/it/contracts.rs:761`) 33 s → 266 s.
* it-2: the test step 240 s → 635 s, mostly `tethers::nothing_in_the_corpus_needs_a_tether` (`tethers.rs:246`) and `sharing::the_one_shared_in_the_repository_comes_out_atomic_undecided` (`sharing.rs:343`).

The commit is 5651724e, "The ledger's panics inference proves a unit through loops, and the lowering takes that proof" (ADR-361 D16, the fix for #2451). Its ×2.7 on `packages/logic` does not explain a ×10, so the first run measured (report of 2026-11-21, parent of 5651724e → develop):

* callgrind of `Ledger::infer` on `packages/logic/src/sv_strategy.nika`: 7.07 G → 49.34 G Ir. `bounds_returns` 6.69 → 47.76 G, of which `bounding_loop_invariant` is 40.76 G (82 %); `bounds_aggressive` only 0.19 → 1.39 G.
* infer per file: `benches/lowering/source.nika` 29.7 → 673 s, 545 s of it in the one function `rs2nika_free_methods` (lines 20045-20259, many loops in sequence and nested, 1.74 M asks); `bounds_walk.nika` 5.2 → 169 s; `sv_sat.nika` 10.9 → 38 s.
* the digest cache `bounds::proven_taken` cannot help: of 11,149 asks, 11,146 have distinct forms.

Two causes are suspected in `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/bounds_walk.nika`, neither settled:

1. `bounding_returns_round` (line 11441) walks every body again in each collect, D32 and keep round, and each walk proves the same loops' invariants again through `bounding_past_loop` → `bounding_loop_invariant` (5679).
2. `bounding_past_loop` (5903) walks the rest of the block again after each settled invariant (ADR-361 D10), so a run of n loops costs about n² walks.

## Decision

Supervisor, 2026-11-21: a settled invariant is a function of the loop and the facts it is entered with, so it is memoized, not proved again. `bounds_returns` keeps, across its rounds, the invariants it settled, keyed by function, loop start and the entry facts (in a canonical form), and a round that enters the same loop with the same facts takes the stored one. Nothing is skipped: a different entry gives a different key and a fresh proof. If (2) still dominates after the cache, the re-walk after a settled loop is cut to what the invariant changed, within ADR-361 D10; if that would change D10's meaning, stop with `Needs: supervisor decision`.

## To build

1. Settle the causes: count `bounding_loop_invariant` calls per (function, loop start) across rounds, and walks per loop in `rs2nika_free_methods`. Put both counts in the report.
2. Build the invariant cache in `bounds_walk.nika` (Nikaia; the lowered file is output). It lives for one `bounds_returns` call, not across programs.
3. If the counts of step 1 show the re-walk of (2) still quadratic, cut it as the Decision says.
4. Add a test in `tests/compiler/tests/` with a `.stdout`: a function with several loops in sequence and nested whose panics inference result is the same as before (the proof unchanged).
5. Measure again with callgrind on both sites above.

## Done when

* Callgrind of `Ledger::infer` on `sv_strategy.nika` is within 1.5× of the parent of 5651724e (≤ 10.6 G Ir), and `rs2nika_free_methods` no longer dominates `source.nika`; or the report shows with figures why not.
* No result of the panics inference changes: the corpus tests pass unchanged.
* A CI run on develop shows heavy-rest and it-2 near their earlier times; the supervisor checks the job durations after the push (builders have no GitHub access).

## Files and limits

* `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/bounds_walk.nika` and its lowered output, `tests/compiler/tests/`; the four tests only to read.
* Do not raise any time limit, skip, split or `#[ignore]` a test, or weaken a proof. Do not take the performance lane's issues.

The D10 re-walk is cut, without losing a proof; this is the main work.** In `bounding_past_loop`, the rest of the block is walked twice, as `leaves` and then as `again`, and each walk carries its own nested re-walks. So a run of n loops costs T(n) = 2·T(n-1). That is 1, 2, 4 … 1024 searches over 14 loops. That is a defect, not a meaning of D10: D10 decides *what* is asked through a loop, not how often the walk visits the rest of a block. The direction:

* `leaves` is walked without its nested re-walks, if `again` (which keeps them) reaches every proof `leaves`' nested walks reached;
* or the re-walk is cut to the statements the invariant's names reach, if nothing outside them can change.

The re-walks of one block must stay linear in the number of loops. Whatever form is chosen, the report argues why it proves exactly what it proved before, not "probably".

# Issue #2477: CI's test shards are balanced by measured duration, not round-robin by name

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2477).

`blocked`, `ci` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-21 · 1 comment

Part of the ci lane's goal, a short CI run.

Facts: CI and caches

After #2474
After #2476

## What happens today

The suite's test shards (`.github/workflows/suite.yml`, matrix `shard`) are uneven. Two recent x86 runs on develop, in seconds:

* `compiler-0..4`: 378 / 377 / 607 / 502 / 440 and 594 / 425 / 623 / 383 / 250.
* `it-0..2`: 394 / 413 / 398 and 360 / 479 / 509.
* `heavy-*` and `ledgers`: 167-253.

The run lasts as long as its slowest shard, so `compiler-2` sets the length at about 610 s while five shards finish under 260 s. `compiler-K` takes every K-th program by sorted name, and `it-K` every K-th short test, so a few long programs landing together make one shard long.

## To build

# Issue #2486: Raw pointers inside `unsafe`: which ones, and what the compiler checks (replacing ADR-302 D9)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2486).

`ffi`, `blocked`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-22 · 2 comments

Decision paper. Nothing here is decided, and no ADR or specification text is written yet.

## Where the question comes from

The owner asked, in a session on Nikaia's place as a systems language (2026-11-19 to 2026-11-21): should a program be able to do everything in Nikaia, raw pointers included, instead of switching to Rust for the last part? The owner's view is that no line needs to be drawn: Rust allows pointers inside `unsafe`, Nikaia already has `unsafe` and already calls C, so a pointer in `unsafe` is no new kind of trust.

Two things already in the repository point the same way:

* [ADR-302](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-302.md) D9 refuses raw pointers, but says itself that the safe forms are "a raw pointer's safe subset, so nothing here is lost the day one is admitted". The door was left open on purpose.
* [ADR-218](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-218.md) puts every `unsafe` topic into a small Rust crate under `crates/unsafe/` (16 crates today, from `tether` to `task-block`). So every new `unsafe` topic is new Rust, which runs against the rule *Written in Nikaia only* (CLAUDE.md).

No program is blocked on this today. The answer decides which way the language grows.

## From zero: what a program can do today

A call into C is written inside `unsafe { … }` (Part III 15.1, ADR-302 D3). A pointer appears only in an `extern` declaration: `ref T`, `ref mut T`, `ref Array[T]` and `ref mut Array[T]` live **for the call** (D5). A length beside a buffer is checked (`NK1159`, D6). A handle from a C library is an `opaque type`, never dereferenced, and released by a cleanup (D7). `unsafe` permits nothing else: "what is inside is checked as anything else is" (D3).

A raw pointer is refused. Run with `target/fast/nikaia check` (built 2026-11-19, tip `e011699a`):

```nika
fn main() throws {
    let p: Pointer[u8]? = null
    println("x")
}
```

```
error[NK1135]: There's no type called `Pointer`.
 2 |     let p: Pointer[u8]? = null
```

So no Nikaia program can build an allocator, an intrusive list, a ring buffer over raw memory, or hand C an address that C keeps past the call. Those live in a Rust crate (ADR-218) or in a described crate ([ADR-rust-boundary-1](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-rust-boundary-1.md)).

## Facts checked in the code

What makes a pointer hard in Nikaia is not the pointer itself. It is that the compiler chooses references and moves the program never writes, and Rust's aliasing rules apply to the Rust it emits.

1. **A changing reference always comes from a written `mut`.** A `mut` parameter, `mut self`, `let mut`, `for mut`, a door of `SharedMut[T]` (Part I 6.3, 6.5). A parameter the body changes without `mut` is `NK1138`. The call site shows nothing (`fill(xs)`), but the declaration does.
2. **A reading reference is often invisible.** A lent parameter may lower to `&T`; a `let` over a place, a `for`, a view handed back are references the source does not spell. In Rust, writing through a raw pointer while a `&T` to the same memory is still used is undefined behaviour.
3. **The compiler moves a value's header (a `String` or `Vec` struct, not its heap data) at points it chooses.** Three cases, read in the lowered Rust:
   * at creation: `let text = __keep.put_viewed(fs::read_to_string(…).await?);` The name exists only as a reference into the anchor, so no pointer can be older than the move;
   * **after the last change** (`late_puts`, `crates/nikaia-std/src/compiler/buffers.nika`). This program, lowered with `nikaia lower`:

     ```nika
     struct View { head: String }

     fn make() -> String {
         let mut g = String()
         g.push_str("  hi  ")
         return g
     }

     fn first_word() -> View {
         let mut text = make()
         text.push_str(" end")
         let w: String = text.trim()
         return View { head: w }
     }

     fn main() throws {
         let v = first_word()
         println(v.head)
     }
     ```

     lowers `first_word` to

     ```rust
     let mut text = make();
     text.push_str(" end"); let text = __keep.put_viewed(text);
     let w: &str = text.trim();
     ```

     and prints `hi   end`. The header moves after the name has existed for two lines. A pointer to `text` taken between them would dangle;
   * moves the program writes (`Cursor { input: text }`, a `keep` parameter), and assigning a variable a new value, where the old buffer moves into the anchor of what holds its views (Part III, `NK2305`).

   After `put_viewed` the header never moves again: the anchor holds an `Arc`, not a `Box`, so that moving the entry touches nothing it points at (`Entry`, `crates/unsafe/tether/src/lib.rs`).
4. **Every one of these points is known while the program is built.** The compiler emits them; `--tethers` prints where each buffer lives. The analysis that refuses a change in place while a view lives (`NK2305`, [ADR-views-3](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-views-3.md) D9) already follows views across these moves.
5. While checking case 3 a lowering defect turned up: a `let mut` whose initialiser can throw gets no late `put_viewed`, and rustc refuses the code (NK1343). Filed as #2465. It does not change the decision, but the build of option C rests on that machinery.

## Options

**A. Nothing: ADR-302 D9 stands.** Pointer code stays in Rust crates (ADR-218) or described crates.
* For: costs nothing; each crate is small, has a README listing every `unsafe` and runs under Miri with both aliasing models (ADR-218 D2); the manifesto's "without `unsafe`" stays trivially true.
* Against: every new `unsafe` topic is new Rust, against *Written in Nikaia only*; a user doing systems work needs two languages; the owner's stated direction is the opposite.

**B. Scoped pointers only.** A pointer exists only inside a block over a place, as Swift's `withUnsafeMutablePointer(to:)`. Proposed syntax, not built:

```nika
unsafe {
    raw::with_address_mut(buffer) { p =>
        p.offset(4).write(0)
    }
}
```

* For: the simplest check: the block holds the place, so nothing moves under the pointer and no view can be used meanwhile.
* Against: a pointer can never be stored, so no allocator, no intrusive structure, no address C keeps. It covers maybe half of what the question is about.

**C. A pointer type, checked where it points into Nikaia's own values, unchecked where it points into raw memory.** Proposed syntax, not built:

```nika
use std::raw

fn fill(mut buf: Vec[u8]) {
    unsafe {
        let p: raw::PointerMut[u8] = raw::address_mut(buf)
        p.offset(1).write(7)
    }
}

fn arena(n: i64) -> raw::PointerMut[u8]? {
    return unsafe { raw::alloc(n) }
}
```

The rules, each read off what the compiler already knows:
1. `Pointer[T]` reads, `PointerMut[T]` reads and writes (the pair `Shared` / `SharedMut` already has). Both are never null; `T?` is the null pointer, one machine word, as for a handle (ADR-302 D11).
2. Taking, reading, writing, offsetting and casting are written inside `unsafe`.
3. `address_mut` takes only a `mut` place (fact 1).
4. **A pointer into a place is valid until the place's next move or its next change by another path**, whether the move is written or inserted (fact 3). Using it after that is refused, the message naming the move and, for an inserted one, the view that made it necessary.
5. A write through a pointer is a change in place of its source: a view of that source still used afterwards is `NK2305`, as today (fact 2).
6. A pointer into a place does not leave the place's scope (returned, kept, given to a task). Refused for now; widening it later is possible, narrowing a free start would not be (ADR-302 D9's own argument).
7. A pointer from `raw::alloc`, from C or from an integer is not checked. That is the part that is `unsafe` in Rust too.
8. A function that writes through a pointer has `touches` *everything* and `locks` *may*, as an `extern` declaration (ADR-302 D4), so the rest of the program stays sound. A `Pointer` does not cross tasks.
9. In an `extern` declaration, a `Pointer[T]` is the address C may keep, beside `ref T` for the call only.

* For: the whole field (allocators, intrusive structures, raw buffers, C keeping an address) can be written in Nikaia; the checked part reuses the views analysis; new `unsafe` topics no longer need new Rust.
* Against: new rules and codes; rule 4 needs the compiler to track every inserted move exactly (fact 5 shows that machinery still has defects); the lowered Rust must stay sound under Rust's aliasing model, which is not final (Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows differ).

**D. Pointers as in Rust, nothing checked.**
* For: smallest compiler work.
* Against: the programmer cannot keep Rust's rules, because the references and moves that break them are not in the source (facts 2 and 3). Undefined behaviour no review can see. Not recommended.

## How other languages do it

* **Rust**: raw pointers `*const T` / `*mut T`; taking one is safe, dereferencing is `unsafe`; nothing is checked; Miri finds undefined behaviour in tests. All references are visible to the programmer, which is what Nikaia does not have.
* **C#**: pointers in `unsafe`; because the garbage collector moves objects, the address of a movable variable can be taken only inside `fixed`, which pins it. The same problem as our moved header, solved by scope.
* **Swift**: `withUnsafePointer(to:)` gives a pointer valid only inside the closure; escaping it is undefined behaviour. Option B.
* **Go**: `unsafe.Pointer` with written rules for `uintptr`, because the runtime moves stacks.
* **Zig**: pointers are ordinary values, `*T` for one element and `[*]T` for many with arithmetic; no hidden moves, so nothing to track.
* **D**: `@system` / `@trusted` / `@safe` on functions; pointers free in `@system`.

## Recommendation

**C.** It is the owner's direction (no line between Nikaia and systems work), and it is the only option where the programmer can actually keep the rules, because the compiler checks exactly the part the programmer cannot see. It also fits [ADR-037](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-037.md) D7: what is observable is written, what is not is inferred, safe as the floor.

Questions the decision should also settle:
* Is taking a pointer inside `unsafe` too (proposed: yes, so all pointer code is visible and countable), or only dereferencing, as in Rust?
* Must a package allow `unsafe` in its dependencies in the manifest, as [ADR-raw-sinks-1](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-raw-sinks-1.md) does for raw sinks? Proposed: yes, and `nikaia` reports how much `unsafe` a package holds.
* Do Nikaia programs with pointer `unsafe` run under Miri in CI, both aliasing models, as the crates of ADR-218 D2 do? Proposed: yes, their lowered Rust.
* ADR-218 stays for existing crates; whether each moves into Nikaia is decided per crate, not here.

## What changes if C is decided

* ADR-302 D9 is replaced by a new decision; Part III 15.1's paragraph *There is no raw pointer* is rewritten; `std::raw` gets its entries.
* New error codes from the block the supervisor reserves.
* The build needs #2465 fixed first.
* The manifesto's claim of benchmarks "without `unsafe`" stays true but needs the `unsafe` count to stay checkable.

## To build

- [ ] The owner chooses A, B, C or D and answers the four questions under *Recommendation*.
- [ ] The deciding session writes the decision as a new ADR that replaces ADR-302 D9, and the specification text (Part III 15.1, the `std::raw` entries, the new codes in Part III's code table), every example run through `scripts/probe.nika --check` on stubs.
- [ ] It files the build as its own `ready` issue with a numbered *To build* list and tests in `tests/compiler/tests/`, naming `Needs #2465`.

## Done when

The owner has decided; the ADR and the specification text are on `develop`; the build issue is filed; or the owner chose A and this issue is closed naming ADR-302 D9.

## Not decided here

The exact names (`raw::address_mut`, `PointerMut`), pointer arithmetic beyond `offset`, volatile access for device registers, and a bare-metal target ([ADR-119](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-119.md)).

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-21](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2486#issuecomment-7059900367)

Owner's answer, 2026-11-21, on the four questions under *Recommendation*: all four as proposed.

1. Taking a pointer is written inside `unsafe` too, not only dereferencing it.
2. A package must allow `unsafe` in its dependencies in the manifest, as ADR-raw-sinks-1 does for raw sinks, and `nikaia` reports how much `unsafe` a package holds.
3. Programs with pointer `unsafe` run under Miri in CI, under both aliasing models, as the crates of ADR-218 D2 do.
4. ADR-218 stays for the existing crates; whether each moves into Nikaia is decided per crate.

The main choice (A, B, C or D) is still to be confirmed.

## What it is

# Issue #2506: Invariant proposers: `nikaia prove --propose` hands open loop problems to outside programs and checks what they answer (ADR-361 D6)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2506).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-21 · 0 comments

Part of #640

## What it is

Outside programs, an LLM among them, may propose loop invariants; the compiler only checks what they propose (ADR-361 D6, Part III 13.2 and 13.3). A proposer is a program named in the manifest's `[prove]` table, run only by `nikaia prove --propose` (or `--propose=CMD` for one run), never by `nikaia build`, `run` or `test`. It runs as a child process with one JSON line per open loop problem each way (ADR-361 D6, round 4, 0.0.998). Every candidate goes through the three-query check of ADR-361 D4 (built in d3d27e2d), and what passes is written to `nikaia.proofs` with the proposer as its origin (the invariant line was built in 2e4328bf).

## To build

1. **The exchange, for one run: `nikaia prove --propose=CMD`.** Start the proposer once as a child process. Write one JSON line per open loop problem to its stdin: `{"version": 1, "id": …, "problem": …, "source": …, "names": […]}`; `problem` is SMT-LIB `HORN`, `source` is the loop's source text, `names` are the names it reads. Close stdin after the last line. Read one JSON line per answer from its stdout: `{"id": …, "candidates": […]}`, each candidate an SMT-LIB term over the names. Show the proposer's stderr to the user. D4 checks each candidate; write the ones that pass to `nikaia.proofs` with the proposer as their origin. Test, with a stub proposer written in Nikaia and run with `nikaia run`: one true and one false candidate, only the true one is written.
2. **A proposer that misbehaves is one helper lost.** Skip a proposer that crashes, ends early, or writes a line in another shape; the other proposers and the built-in strategies continue. Tests with the stub proposer: a proposer that crashes, the run continues; a line in the wrong shape is skipped; an unknown `version` is refused with a message.
3. **The manifest: `[prove] proposers = ["cmd arg", …]` and `nikaia prove --propose`.** Tests: `nikaia build` never starts a proposer; `--locked` reads the written entry.

## Done when

`nikaia prove --propose=CMD` and `nikaia prove --propose` with `[prove] proposers` hand each open loop problem to the proposers as JSON lines, write only candidates that pass the three queries to `nikaia.proofs` with the proposer as origin, survive a proposer that crashes or answers in another shape, and `nikaia build` never starts one, each shown by the tests above; the last commit carries `Fixes` for this issue and the report has a `Found:` line per finding.

# Issue #2510: When does the prover take up PDR/IC3 for loops? (ADR-361 D5 item 5)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2510).

`decision` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-21 · 0 comments

Part of #640
After #2507

## What it is

ADR-361 D5 item 5 puts property-directed reachability (PDR/IC3) on Horn clauses last in the prover's portfolio, "when the methods before it are exhausted and the solver is ready for it"; D8 says "PDR when D5 says". ADR-361 §2 rates it the strongest single method for integers, directed at the claim, but large to build, able to search without end, with invariants hard to read. Nobody has decided yet what counts as "exhausted" and "ready", so nobody can queue the build.

## The question

When does the prover take up PDR/IC3, and what shows that the methods before it are exhausted and the solver is ready?

Options the text gives:
- **A.** Once the strategies before it (closed forms, intervals and octagons, k-induction, guess and check) are built, as the next step of D5's order.
- **B.** Only when claims in our own code are found that every built strategy leaves open, so that PDR has work the others cannot do.
- **C.** Not built in our solver: a proposer (ADR-361 D6, "another solver that already does what D5 has not built yet") brings PDR's invariants from an outside Horn solver, checked by D4.

## To build

1. The supervisor or the owner picks an option above and records it in ADR-361 D5; then a build issue is filed for PDR, or none if C is picked.

## Done when

ADR-361 D5 states when PDR/IC3 is built, and a build issue for it exists or the ADR says none is needed.

# Issue #2518: A type whose `mut self` method throws keeps its rule as a fact: the rule is checked before each call that may fail

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2518).

`blocked`, `solver` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-23 · 3 comments

Part of #714

## What it is

A struct whose method changes `self` and `throws` keeps no rule as a fact today (98a8e39a, ADR-369 D3): a failing call left the method with the rule broken, and the caller could catch the error and go on. Such a type could keep its facts if the rule were checked at each call inside the method that may fail, so the rule holds at every `throw` as ADR-369 D2 requires. That needs the pass to know which calls fail. Governing decision: ADR-369 D2 (the rule holds at each `return` and each `throw` of a method that changes the value) and D3.

## To build

1. **The rule is checked before each call that may fail in a `mut self` method that throws**, and the type keeps its rule as a fact at entry (the entry fact 98a8e39a drops comes back). Test in `tests/compiler/tests/`: a `mut self` method that breaks the rule, then calls a throwing function, and a caller that catches the error and indexes with the rule's bound: the check fires with the rule's message before the call; with the rule restored before the call, the index is proved.

## Done when

A type with a `mut self` method that throws keeps its written rule as a fact at its methods' entries, and a test shows the rule checked before a call that may fail and the caller's index proved; the commit carries this issue's `Fixes` line.

`decision`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-21 · 0 comments

Part of #743
After #743

## What it is
ADR-374 D8: a cut at proven positions is not checked at run time; both ends are positions of the text by D1 and D5, so the cut is the slice. Today every `before`/`after`/`between`/`split_at` keeps Rust's boundary check (run reports of 71a74e37 and 6bbfac8b), because nothing yet rules out that the text changed while a position of it lived.

**Open question** (raised by the run of 6bbfac8b; ADR-374 does not say): what keeps a position valid when its text is changed (a `mut` text pushed to or cleared) while the position lives?
- (a) A `Pos` holds its text as a view holds its source (D5 says it "carries sources as a view does", Part I 6.6), so a change to the text while a position of it lives is refused, and D8 drops the check everywhere.
- (b) D8 drops the check only where the compiler sees the text unchanged between taking the position and the cut; elsewhere the check stays.

## To build
1. Once decided: a cut at positions the checker followed to its own text (D5) lowers to the plain slice with no boundary check. Test: a cut at proven positions emits no boundary check (look at the lowering), plus the refusal or kept check the decision names.

## Done when
The question above is answered in ADR-374, and a cut at proven positions lowers without `is_char_boundary`, shown by its test; the commit carries `Fixes #N` for this issue, and the report gives a `Found:` line per finding.

# Issue #2552: Decision: does the prover derive what a function hands back as a fact for its callers (call results, ~60 sites of claim (b))

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2552).

`decision` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-21 · 0 comments

Part of #1053

## What it is

About 60 unproved sites in the compiler's Nikaia code stand under the reason *a call's result* (figure of 2026-10-31 in #1053: 60 under `prove-through-loops:on`); an example is a function that returns an index or -1 (`the_boundary`, named in "Bounds reasons: split the catch-all by the form that blocks a site" #1105). The prover needs a fact about what the callee hands back. #1053 step 6 marked this "postconditions on a program's own function: needs a decision paper when reached". What is decided: a written `assert` before `return` is a postcondition, published as `ensures` (ADR-269 D17, D18); a private function takes as facts what all its callers prove about its arguments (ADR-391 D1, derived preconditions). No decision yet derives a postcondition from a body without a written `assert`, and #1053's rule (owner, 2026-11-08) forbids writing an `assert` into the compiler's code only to raise the figure.

The question: where a function no other package can call hands back a value its body bounds (every exit returns `-1` or an index below a list's length), does the prover derive that as a fact for its callers?

Options the text gives:

- **A. Derived from the body**, bottom-up over the call graph and kept as ADR-391 D3 keeps derived facts, as Infer derives pre- and postconditions per procedure (ADR-391 §2); derived, not promised (ADR-391 D4).
- **B. Written only**: the author states the postcondition with an `assert` before `return` (ADR-269 D17); the call-result sites of the compiler stay unproved until a written postcondition is an interface rule.

## To build

1. **A decision paper**: the two options with a probe of one real call-result site each, a recommendation, and, once decided, the ADR text and the build issue it files.

## Done when

The question is decided (the ADR decision named) and its build is filed as its own issue, or this issue is closed naming why no build is needed.

# Issue #2575: A program can hold a raw pointer inside `unsafe`: `raw::Pointer[T]`, `raw::PointerMut[T]` and their checks (ADR-pointers-v1)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/2575).

`compiler`, `ffi`, `blocked`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-21 · updated 2026-11-22 · 1 comment

Builds [ADR-pointers-v1](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-pointers-v1.md) and [ADR-c-boundary-v1](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-c-boundary-v1.md) D9, as Part III 15.1 states them.

Part of #2486
Needs #2465

## The goal

A program can hold a raw pointer inside `unsafe`. Today `raw::Pointer[u8]` is refused (`NK1135`, "There's no type called `Pointer`", `target/fast/nikaia check`, tip `e2c62d70`), and an allocator, an intrusive structure or an address C keeps must be written in Rust. After this, Part III 15.1's example runs:

```nika
use std::raw

fn fill(mut buf: Vec[u8]) {
    unsafe {
        let p: raw::PointerMut[u8] = raw::address_mut(buf[0])
        p.offset(1).write(7)
    }
}

fn main() throws {
    let mut buf: Vec[u8] = [0, 0, 0]
    fill(buf)
    println(f"{buf[1]}")
}
```

and prints `7`.

## The governing decision
